entity.name: Hammurabi
entity.description: The king who carved 282 laws into stone and changed justice forever. Sixth king of Babylon's First Dynasty, Hammurabi transformed a minor city-state into an empire spanning all of Mesopotamia. His law code, inscribed on a black diorite stele, introduced the presumption of innocence and was declared by the god Shamash himself.

story.name: Hammurabi
story.description: Inheriting a minor city-state, crushing Elam and Larsa, conquering all of Mesopotamia, then inscribing 282 laws on a stele for all to see. The king who wrote civilization's rules in stone.

moments.name: Hammurabi Inherits the Throne of a Minor City-State Called Babylon
moments.subtitle: Overshadowed by Elam, Assyria, and Larsa, this small kingdom will soon swallow them all
moments.description: Around 1792 BC, Hammurabi inherited the throne of Babylon from his ailing father Sin-Muballit. At the time, Babylon was a minor Amorite city-state that controlled little territory beyond its walls, overshadowed by the powerful kingdoms of Elam, Assyria, Eshnunna, and Larsa. The city had been founded only about a century earlier in 1894 BC. Hammurabi's father had begun consolidating nearby territories, conquering Borsippa, Kish, and Sippar. Within three decades, Hammurabi would transform this modest inheritance into the dominant power of Mesopotamia, uniting the entire region under Babylonian rule.

moments.name: Hammurabi Conquers Larsa and Seizes Control of All Lower Mesopotamia
moments.subtitle: An ally's betrayal gives the Babylonian king the excuse he needs to attack
moments.description: Around 1763 BC, Hammurabi conquered the kingdom of Larsa after its king failed to provide adequate military support during the war against Elam. Hammurabi and Larsa had allied to crush the Elamite invasion of the Mesopotamian plain, but Larsa's contribution was minimal. Angered by this betrayal, Hammurabi turned on his former ally and captured the entire lower Mesopotamian plain. This conquest was the turning point of Hammurabi's reign, transforming Babylon from a regional power into the dominant force in southern Mesopotamia. Within a few more years, Hammurabi would conquer Eshnunna, Mari, and subdue Assyria.

moments.name: Hammurabi Inscribes 282 Laws on a Stone Stele and Displays It Publicly
moments.subtitle: The code introduces the presumption of innocence and eye-for-an-eye justice
moments.description: During his reign (c. 1792-1750 BC), Hammurabi commissioned a black diorite stele inscribed with 282 laws covering everything from property disputes to medical malpractice, written in Akkadian so any literate Babylonian could read it. A carving at the top depicts Hammurabi receiving the laws from Shamash, the god of justice. The Code of Hammurabi was among the first to establish the presumption of innocence, prescribe specific penalties for specific crimes, and limit retribution. The stele was later plundered by the Elamites and taken to Susa, where French archaeologists rediscovered it in 1901. It now stands in the Louvre.

moments.name: Archaeologists Rediscover Hammurabi's Law Code Stele in the Ruins of Susa
moments.subtitle: A 3,700-year-old stone monument resurfaces in Iran, rewriting the history of law
moments.description: In 1901, a French archaeological expedition led by Jacques de Morgan discovered the Code of Hammurabi stele in the ruins of Susa, the ancient Elamite capital in present-day Iran. The Elamites had plundered the 2.25-meter-tall black diorite stele from Babylon centuries after Hammurabi's reign. The discovery revealed 282 laws that predated the Law of Moses and demonstrated a sophisticated legal tradition in ancient Mesopotamia. The stele was transported to the Louvre Museum in Paris, where it remains one of the most visited ancient artifacts. Hammurabi's image now appears in courthouses worldwide, including the U.S. Supreme Court.

moments.name: Hammurabi Dies and His Empire Immediately Begins to Collapse
moments.subtitle: His son inherits all of Mesopotamia, but it will not hold together for long
moments.description: Around 1750 BC, Hammurabi died and passed the throne to his son Samsu-iluna, under whose rule the Babylonian empire quickly began to unravel. Hammurabi had unified all of Mesopotamia through a combination of military conquest, strategic alliances, and administrative skill, forcing even the Assyrian king to pay tribute. But the empire he built was held together largely by his personal authority. Within a generation, native Akkadian speakers would throw off Babylonian rule in both the north and south. Despite the empire's collapse, Hammurabi's legacy as a lawgiver endured for millennia, and later Mesopotamian kings claimed descent from him.
